hints: Hint 1: Think about what carries the signal in each case - light in glass versus electric current in copper - and what that means for how much information can be sent per second.
Hint 2: Think about how the signal weakens with distance and how outside electrical disturbances affect a metal wire but not a glass fibre.
Hint 3: Think about practical issues for long cables - size, weight, cost - and also about whether the signal can leak out or be picked up secretly.
parts.proper_answer: Any three from: greater bandwidth; immune to e.m. interference; less attenuation so fewer repeaters needed; greater security / less cross-talk / less power radiated; lighter, cheaper, smaller and easier to handle.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why Fibre Carries More Information**
Light in an optic fibre has a very much higher frequency than electrical signals in a wire. That means you can modulate it at a much higher rate. So one clear advantage is greater bandwidth, meaning more data per second.

Step 2: **Why Fibre Is Cleaner and Travels Further**
A metal wire picks up electromagnetic noise from motors, power lines and other wires. A glass fibre carries light, not current, so it does not suffer from e.m. interference. It also has much less attenuation, so the signal stays strong over long distances and fewer amplifiers or repeaters are needed.

Step 3: **Why Fibre Is More Practical and Secure**
For the third point, pick any other practical benefit. Fibre is thinner, lighter, cheaper and occupies less space. Also very little energy is radiated from the fibre, so there is less cross-talk between fibres and much better security against tapping.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Start by working out the total loss in dB for the whole 57 km link from the given loss per km.
Hint 2: Link that total dB loss to the input and output powers using the $10 \log$ power-ratio relation, remembering that attenuation means input power is larger than output power.
parts.proper_answer: Total attenuation $= 0.50 \times 57 = 28.5\text{ dB} = 10 \log(15 \times 10^{-3} / P)$, giving $P = 2.1 \times 10^{-5}\text{ W}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the Total Loss in dB**
Attenuation adds up along the fibre. You are given $0.50\text{ dB km}^{-1}$ and length $57\text{ km}$, so total attenuation is simply:
$$ \text{attenuation} = 0.50 \times 57 = 28.5\text{ dB} $$

Step 2: **Convert dB to Power Ratio**
For power, the decibel definition is:
$$ \text{attenuation (dB)} = 10 \log \left( \frac{P_{in}}{P_{out}} \right) $$
Here $P_{in} = 15 \times 10^{-3}\text{ W}$ and $P_{out} = P$. So:
$$ 28.5 = 10 \log \left( \frac{15 \times 10^{-3}}{P} \right) $$
$$ \log \left( \frac{15 \times 10^{-3}}{P} \right) = 2.85 $$
$$ \frac{15 \times 10^{-3}}{P} = 10^{2.85} \approx 708 $$
$$ P = \frac{15 \times 10^{-3}}{708} \approx 2.1 \times 10^{-5}\text{ W} $$
That matches the value to be shown.

parts.label: (b)(ii)

markscheme_points.text: $14 < 24$ or S/N ratio < minimum S/N ratio
so not able to distinguish signal from noise
(calculation of minimum acceptable power at receiver)
so not able to distinguish signal from noise

hints: Hint 1: Recall how signal-to-noise ratio in dB is defined from the signal power you just found and the given noise power at the receiver.
Hint 2: Work out the actual S/N value in dB and place it side-by-side with the required minimum of 24 dB.
Hint 3: Decide what that comparison means physically for whether the receiver electronics can pick out the real signal.
parts.proper_answer: S/N $= 10 \log(2.1 \times 10^{-5} / 9.0 \times 10^{-7}) \approx 14\text{ dB} < 24\text{ dB}$. Signal power is below minimum acceptable, so receiver is not able to distinguish signal from noise.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Calculate the Actual S/N Ratio**
Signal-to-noise ratio compares how strong your wanted signal is against the background hiss. In dB:
$$ \text{S/N (dB)} = 10 \log \left( \frac{P_{signal}}{P_{noise}} \right) $$
Put in $P_{signal} = 2.1 \times 10^{-5}\text{ W}$ and $P_{noise} = 9.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ W}$:
$$ \text{S/N} = 10 \log \left( \frac{2.1 \times 10^{-5}}{9.0 \times 10^{-7}} \right) $$
$$ \text{S/N} = 10 \log(23.3) \approx 13.7\text{ dB} \approx 14\text{ dB} $$

Step 2: **Compare With the Minimum Needed**
You need at least $24\text{ dB}$ for reliable detection. Here:
$$ 14\text{ dB} < 24\text{ dB} $$
Equivalently, the minimum acceptable signal power would be $P_{min}$ from $24 = 10 \log(P_{min} / 9.0 \times 10^{-7})$, giving $P_{min} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{-4}\text{ W}$, which is about ten times larger than the actual $2.1 \times 10^{-5}\text{ W}$.

Step 3: **Make the Decision**
Because the actual signal is too close in size to the noise, the receiver cannot reliably tell them apart. So the answer is no, the receiver is not able to distinguish the signal from the noise. An amplifier or repeater would be needed.

parts.label: (b)
parts.question_text:
An optic fibre of length 57 km is connected between a transmitter and a receiver, as shown in
Fig. 5.1.
The attenuation per unit length of the optic fibre is 0.50 dB km⁻¹. The transmitter provides an
input signal of power 15 × 10⁻³ W to the fibre. The noise power at the receiver is 9.0 × 10⁻⁷ W.

The attenuation per unit length of the optic fibre is $0.50\text{ dB km}^{-1}$. The transmitter provides an input signal of power $15 \times 10^{-3}\text{ W}$ to the fibre. The noise power at the receiver is $9.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ W}$.
